name: lexy
workload: JSON validation (accept/reject, no DOM construction) of three real-world files from the nativejson-benchmark corpus (canada.json, citm_catalog.json, twitter.json), timed with nanobench
claimed_speedup: ~1.6x-2.2x lower validation time than PEGTL across the three test files (derived from page data: canada.json lexy median ~2.25ms vs pegtl ~3.65ms [1.62x]; citm_catalog.json lexy ~1.08ms vs pegtl ~2.37ms [2.19x]; twitter.json lexy ~0.75ms vs pegtl ~1.41ms [1.88x])
tradeoffs: lexy parses via callbacks straight into user-supplied types (zero-copy) rather than a generic DOM; its DSL is more verbose than PEGTL's template-class grammar; requires C++17; the benchmark measures pure validation, not full parsing into a data structure, so results may not generalize.
caveats: First-party benchmark run by the lexy author, not an independent suite; the page states hardware (M1 Mac Mini) and the harness (nanobench) but not the compiler or optimization flags used, which caps the tier below A; PEGTL was fetched from its 'main' branch at benchmark-run time rather than a pinned release; a Boost.JSON series is defined in the benchmark's CMakeLists but did not appear in the rendered results for these three files.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "parser combinator" -> foonathan/lexy README FAQ "How fast is it?" -> benchmarks/json/ directory and lexy.foonathan.net/benchmark_json/

name: re2c
workload: Generated-lexer execution speed on ~15 real-world and synthetic regex/grammar workloads (HTTP header parsing per RFC7230, email address, datetime-to-JSON, URI per RFC3986, Apache log lines, plus synthetic alternation/repetition patterns), each compiled with re2c vs Ragel under GCC-14.2.0 and Clang-19.1.4 at -O3
claimed_speedup: ~1.0x-1.4x lower CPU time than Ragel on most real-world text-format workloads (derived from page data, e.g. http-rfc7230/gcc: re2c 21.2 vs ragel 25.5 [1.20x]; email/gcc ~1.32x; datetime/gcc ~1.36x); on several synthetic deeply-nested repetition/alternation patterns (rep-*, rep-alt-*) re2c is instead 1.5x-4x SLOWER than Ragel
hardware: Intel Core i7-8750H, 6 cores, 32 GiB RAM (per benchmarks/c/results/env_20250131.rst)
tradeoffs: re2c emits inline conditional-jump state machines instead of table-driven code, which can grow generated code size for large grammars; it requires hand-writing the driver/interface code around the generated lexer; results are workload-dependent rather than a uniform win.
caveats: Baseline is Ragel, not Flex/Bison/ANTLR/Boost.Spirit -- none of those four appear in re2c's own benchmark suite. Results are mixed: real-world-shaped grammars mostly favor re2c (~1.0-1.4x) but several synthetic repetition-heavy patterns favor Ragel by 1.5-4x, so 'faster' does not hold universally. GitHub reports re2c's license as 'Other/NOASSERTION' because its bespoke public-domain-style LICENSE text is not a registered SPDX id (no patent grant); recorded as usability=copyable per the public-domain rule.
found_via: GitHub: known project re2c -> repo benchmarks/c/results/results_20250131.json and env_20250131.rst (cross-checked against benchmarks/_engines/ragel)

name: chumsky
workload: Idiomatic JSON parsing benchmark (single document) compared across 8 Rust parsing libraries/hand-written parser, single core
claimed_speedup: chumsky (check-only): 797 MB/s (140.77us) vs nom: 213 MB/s (526.52us) => ~3.7x higher throughput; chumsky (full parse): 533 MB/s (210.43us) => ~2.5x higher throughput than nom (numbers as published in the README performance table)
hardware: single core of an AMD Ryzen 7 3700x
tradeoffs: Single micro-benchmark (JSON); chumsky's own README warns results vary heavily with grammar shape and that 'chumsky is faster than X' is too strong a claim from one workload; check-only mode (the fastest number) does validation without building a parse tree.
caveats: Repository is archived on GitHub (archived=true) even though its last commit is fairly recent, so it will receive no further updates; compiler version and optimization flags for the benchmark are not stated on the page, only the CPU; this is the project's own first-party benchmark.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "parser combinator" -> zesterer/chumsky README "## Performance" section

name: winnow
workload: Same idiomatic JSON parsing benchmark as the chumsky shootout (single document), single core
claimed_speedup: 627 MB/s (178.91us) vs nom's 213 MB/s (526.52us) => ~2.9x higher throughput (numbers as published in a third-party shootout table in the chumsky README, not in winnow's own docs)
hardware: single core of an AMD Ryzen 7 3700x
tradeoffs: winnow is a nom-derived combinator library aimed at ergonomics as much as raw speed; the win here comes from a shootout run and published by a different project (chumsky), not from winnow's own benchmark suite, and was not independently re-run in this search; winnow's own 'Why winnow?' docs page makes no numeric speed claim over nom.
caveats: Harvested from a third-party shootout (chumsky's README), not winnow's own claim; compiler version/flags not stated; single JSON workload only, may not generalize to other grammars.
found_via: GitHub: harvested from zesterer/chumsky README performance shootout table while researching "parser combinator faster" via gh search repos
